21.t: Working with data: predator and prey numbers
q: Describe the pattern in hare numbers.
Numbers rise and fall in cycles of about 12 years, with peaks of about 75–80 thousand at years 4 and 16.
Estimate the time lag between hare peaks and lynx peaks.
About 2 years.
Explain why lynx peaks follow hare peaks.
Plenty of prey lets more lynx survive and breed, so lynx rise a little later; then hares crash and lynx starve, so lynx fall too.
Hare numbers also cycle on islands with no lynx. Suggest what this shows.
Other factors also control hares: food shortage from overgrazing, disease, other predators. Lynx are not the only cause.
These numbers come from fur traders’ records. Suggest one weakness of the data.
Trapping effort changed with fur prices, so the numbers trapped are not a true count of the populations.
Describe the effect of removing Balanus on Chthamalus on the lower shore.
Survival rose from 10% to 70%: seven times higher.
Deduce the fundamental and realised niches of Chthamalus.
Fundamental: upper and lower shore. Realised: upper shore only, when Balanus is present.
Suggest why Balanus survives poorly on the upper shore.
It cannot tolerate drying out when exposed to air for long periods at low tide: an abiotic limit.
Name the principle shown, and explain it.
Competitive exclusion: where both can live, Balanus grows faster and crowds out or crushes Chthamalus, so the two cannot share the same niche.
Explain why the experiment used many plots.
Survival varies between plots; repeats give more reliable means and show whether differences are real.
